messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 68, Darnell had built much of his life around movement. An African American dancer who had spent decades performing, teaching, and keeping his body conditioned, he had always trusted rhythm, timing, and the feel of a room. That changed after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that occurred on a routine drive home. He was traveling in his own lane when another car struck him hard enough to send the vehicle spinning and stop traffic around him. In the aftermath, he remembered flashes rather than a continuous sequence: the jolt of impact, the sound of metal, a glimpse of faces, the confusion of being moved and spoken to, and then long stretches that remained blank. Even soon afterward, when others asked him to explain what had happened, he found he could not tell a clear story. The memory seemed to come in broken pieces, and when he tried to deliberately summon it, the details would not stay in view. What was left felt like an incomplete picture, with missing sections he could not fill in no matter how hard he tried.

In the weeks and months that followed, Darnell began to organize his days around avoiding reminders and circumstances that left him feeling exposed. He went out less and less, telling himself that staying home was simpler and safer than facing the unpredictability of the outside world. Social contacts narrowed noticeably, especially with people he had once socialized with before the accident. Invitations from fellow dancers, old colleagues, and friends who had known him in a more outgoing period often sat unanswered. He did not want to be put in the position of talking about the crash, and he also did not want to be seen as fragile by people who remembered him as capable and physically assured. Even in therapy, he found himself steering away from anything that had been discussed too directly, avoiding thinking about it afterward and sometimes coming away irritated with himself for having opened the subject at all.

His sense of safety became tied to where he sat. In waiting rooms, restaurants, and rehearsal spaces, Darnell sought out chairs against a wall so he could see the room. If he was seated where people were behind him, he felt unsettled and watched the entrance, the exits, and anyone moving quickly through the space. Unexpected or loud sounds kept him on guard. A sudden bang from a dropped pan in the kitchen, a car horn outside his apartment, or the sharp clatter of equipment in a studio would make him tense immediately, as if something dangerous were about to happen. Delays also became hard to tolerate. If a ride took longer than it should, if someone was late, or if an expected call did not come through, he assumed something bad was happening before there was any evidence of it. He found himself scanning for the worst in ordinary pauses, unable to settle until the uncertainty was resolved.

Darnell also came to doubt himself in ways that were deeply distressing to him. He had once relied on quick judgment in performance and in daily life, but after the collision he began to fear that he could not trust himself to do the right thing. That worry showed up in small decisions, from navigating a crosswalk to planning an outing, and it left him second-guessing choices he would previously have made automatically. More unsettling still was the sense that he could no longer trust his own body. As a dancer, his body had been both instrument and identity, but now he saw it as unreliable, unpredictable, and no longer fully under his control. Even ordinary bodily sensations could make him feel vulnerable, as though the vehicle of his life had become less dependable than he had ever imagined. Beneath that sat a deeper disappointment in the people and systems that should have kept him safe. He had come to believe that the institutions involved failed him at the moment he needed protection most, and that sense of being let down lingered whenever he thought about what should have happened differently.

By the time he sought help, Darnell was still living with the same broken and vivid fragments of the crash, the same difficulty making sense of it, and the same sharp unease in public places. The changes had begun to interfere with the life he once led with ease: he was out less, seen less, and less connected to the dance community that had long been central to him. He came to treatment not because he expected the memories to disappear, but because he was tired of feeling on edge in his own body and in ordinary rooms, and tired of shrinking his world to avoid what might unsettle him. What he feared most was that he would never again trust himself, his body, or the world enough to move through life the way he used to. What he hoped for was more modest but deeply important to him: to make sense of what happened, to stop feeling so unsafe, and to return to some version of himself that could sit in a room, go outside, and be with other people without constantly bracing for the next thing to go wrong.
